input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "I hired Mara Venn to restore a walnut drop-leaf table that had belonged to my grandparents. It had spent years in a damp storage unit, and the finish was cloudy, one rear leg rocked, and the left leaf sagged whenever anyone leaned on it. I wanted to use it again for Sunday dinners, but I did not want it made to look new. The scratches and small dents were part of its history, and I said that plainly during our first meeting.

Mara came to my apartment to examine the table before giving me an estimate. She checked the hinges, tapped along the apron, and looked underneath with a small flashlight. She pointed out an old repair near the central stretcher, where someone had driven a pair of mismatched screws into the wood. “Those are holding for now,” she said, “but they’re not doing the joint any favors.” She also explained that the cloudy surface might be wax buildup rather than damage to the finish itself. I appreciated that she did not promise a dramatic transformation before she had tested anything.

The estimate separated the work into a few parts: stabilize the rear leg, adjust the leaf supports, clean the surface, and apply a fresh protective coat if the existing finish allowed it. It also listed the cost of replacing the hinges as an optional item. Mara said she would try cleaning and adjusting them first, then call me if replacement seemed necessary. I agreed to that plan. The written estimate was clear about the labor charge and the price of materials, and it gave a two-week window rather than a guaranteed completion date.

1. The repair process

Mara took the table to her workshop and sent me photographs after the first inspection. In one picture, she had removed the loose screws and was testing a small patch of finish on the underside of the top. In another, she showed the leaf resting on its support. The support was slightly twisted, but not cracked. She told me the table would need a new wooden shim and a careful adjustment, not a replacement part. That matched what I had hoped for, since I wanted as much of the original construction kept as possible.

A few days later, she called to say the surface cleaned up better than expected. The cloudy areas were mostly old wax, though there were still pale rings near one corner. She asked whether I wanted those rings reduced as far as possible or left visible. I asked her to reduce them without sanding away the surrounding finish. She said she could improve them, but could not promise they would disappear. The final result followed that limit: the rings are fainter, and I can still see them when the light hits at an angle.

When I visited the workshop, Mara showed me the repaired leg and explained how she had secured the joint. She had used a fitted hardwood insert where the old screws had loosened the wood, then clamped the joint while the adhesive cured. The repair is not visible from a normal standing position, and the table no longer wobbles on my floor. She also showed me the shim beneath the leaf support. It sits out of sight, and the leaf now rests level with the center section.

The hinges did not need replacing after all. Mara cleaned them, tightened the fasteners, and checked that both leaves opened without catching. One hinge still makes a small click at the end of its movement, something she mentioned before I collected the table. She said she could look at it again if it worsened, but did not think the sound affected the hinge’s function. I liked that she brought it up instead of letting me discover it later and wonder whether it had been overlooked.

2. The finished table

The table came back with a soft sheen, not a glossy, factory-like surface. The grain is easier to see now, especially across the center panel, but the old scratches remain. A shallow dent near the edge is still there, as are two darker marks on one leaf. Those details make the table look like the same piece I brought in, only cleaner and more stable. Mara had been careful to keep the color consistent, although the repaired area underneath is a little lighter than the surrounding wood. No one would notice it unless they looked for it.

We tested the table together in my dining room. Both leaves opened smoothly, and the supports held them without shifting. I placed a stack of plates on the left leaf and pressed gently near its outer edge. It stayed level. Mara advised me to use coasters and wipe spills promptly, which seemed sensible for a table with an older finish. She also left a small card listing the materials she had used and the date of the final coat.

The project took a little over two weeks, within the window in the estimate. Mara kept me updated without sending a message every day, and she asked before making the one decision that could have changed the table’s appearance. Her workshop was tidy when I visited, and she wrapped the top carefully for the trip back. The final invoice matched the estimate because the optional hinge replacement was not needed.

I have used the table for several Sunday dinners since then. It is sturdy enough for ordinary meals, and the leaves no longer feel like something I should avoid touching. I would recommend Mara to someone who wants a thoughtful repair rather than a complete cosmetic makeover. She explained what she could do, what might remain visible, and why she chose each repair. Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "i had been looking at the walnut sideboard in my aunt's back room for years, but this spring i finally asked if i could work on it. she said yes, with the condition that i not make it look new. the piece is about five feet long, has two doors and three drawers, and sits on short turned feet. the top had pale rings from flowerpots and a dark patch near the left edge. one door hung lower than the other, though it still closed. i had never restored a sideboard before, and i was not sure how much of the old finish i could save.

my aunt remembered buying it secondhand in 1988, after moving into her first apartment. she did not know who made it or what year it was from. there was no label on the back, only a pencil mark that looked like “17B.” i took a few photographs before moving it, including one of the loose brass pull on the top drawer. the drawer fronts were not perfectly even, and the right door had a shallow dent. those marks mattered to her, so i wrote them down rather than treating them as damage to erase. i also put small numbered labels on the hinges, because i thought they might not be interchangeable.

1. First inspection and preparation

I set the sideboard in my garage, where the floor is level, and checked each part before taking anything apart. the left rear foot rocked slightly, while the other three felt stable. one screw on the lower hinge was partly stripped, and the door had a narrow gap along its top edge. i found dust and a few dry leaves inside the cabinet, but no smell of dampness. after removing the drawers, i vacuumed the corners with a brush attachment and wiped the inside with a barely damp cloth. i did not use water on the veneer. the veneer at the back corner was lifting, and i decided to leave it alone until i understood how far the loose section went.

my neighbor leah stopped by while i was looking at the drawer runners. she said, “That top has seen a lot of tea cups.” i laughed, because the rings were in exactly the places where my aunt keeps setting her mug. i told leah i was hoping to keep the marks from the sideboard’s life, not just its color. that was an easy thing to say, but harder when i started sanding a test patch and saw how quickly the finish changed. the patch was on the underside of the top, where it would not show. i stopped before going any farther and checked with my aunt by phone. she said, “Please don’t chase every spot. I like that it’s been used.”

I tried a mild furniture cleaner first, using a soft cotton cloth and working on a small area at a time. the cloth picked up brown residue, but the pale rings did not disappear. i waited for the test area to dry before applying a little paste wax. it looked less dull, although the dark patch remained. i was unsure whether the patch was a stain in the wood or something sitting on the finish, so i did not scrape it. the sides needed only cleaning, but the top seemed to need a more careful decision. i kept notes about which products i used and where, partly because i was worried i would forget what i had already tried.

2. Small repairs, not a makeover

I removed the loose brass pull and cleaned it with a dry cloth. i did not polish it, because its darker color matched the other two pulls. for the stripped hinge screw, i used a slightly wider screw of the same general type that i had in my repair box. it caught in the wood, but i could not tell whether it would hold up to years of use. the door sat more evenly afterward, though there was still a small gap at the top. i tightened the remaining hinge screws without forcing them. i also put a thin layer of glue under the lifted veneer at the back corner and held it flat with a padded block and a clamp. i left it clamped overnight, then checked that the edge was no longer raised.

the left rear foot still rocked, so i looked underneath for a loose joint. i could not see a crack, and none of the other feet moved when i pressed them. i slipped a small felt pad under that foot rather than taking the base apart. the sideboard stood steadily on the garage floor after that, but i do not know how it will behave on my aunt’s older kitchen floor. i told her about the pad and the replacement screw before bringing the piece back. she asked if the dent in the right door was still visible, and i said yes. she seemed relieved, which made me think i had understood her request correctly, though i was still learning where restoration ends and changing a piece begins.

when i returned the sideboard, my aunt opened each drawer and shut it again. the middle one stuck slightly at first, then slid more smoothly after i brushed dust from its runner. she looked at the top for a while and said, “It still feels like mine.” i took that as a kind response, not a technical assessment. the flowerpot rings are still there, and so is the dark patch. the repaired veneer is less noticeable from standing height, but i can find it if i look closely. i felt pleased that the sideboard was cleaner and steadier, while also aware that the work had not answered every question about its age, wood, or finish. Customer service replied in the chat after about twelve minutes and offered me an eight-dollar credit, which I have not used yet. Delivery fees also add up when I order small amounts, so I have been trying to plan larger orders instead.
